Family Health

Diclofenac suppositories during breastfeeding

Updated: October 11, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Diclofenac reduces pain and inflammation. Current breastfeeding guidance generally considers it an appropriate option when clinically needed, particularly for a healthy baby born at term. That does not make every product or dose suitable for everyone: the parent’s health, other medicines and the baby’s circumstances still matter.

What diclofenac treats

Diclofenac is a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug, or NSAID. Oral medicines, injections, skin preparations and rectal suppositories are available under various brands. Their doses, uses and instructions differ; do not substitute forms or combine them without checking the total dose with a clinician or pharmacist.

Depending on the product and clinical situation, it may be used for inflammatory joint disease, osteoarthritis, gout, ankylosing spondylitis, back or other musculoskeletal pain, dental pain, selected migraine treatment, painful periods or pain after childbirth or surgery. A suppository is absorbed into the bloodstream: using the rectal route does not remove stomach, kidney, bleeding or cardiovascular risks.

What current breastfeeding advice says

NHS and Specialist Pharmacy Service advice supports diclofenac when appropriate during breastfeeding; ibuprofen and diclofenac are preferred NSAID options in SPS guidance. Milk levels appear low, although published evidence is limited. Use the lowest effective dose for the shortest necessary time, with a clear reason for treatment. It is not reserved only for situations where every alternative has failed.

SPS recommendations mainly apply to healthy infants born at term. LactMed’s July 2026 review notes that alternatives with more evidence may be preferred for a newborn or premature baby. Seek individual advice if the baby is premature, unwell or very young, or if several medicines are being taken. Low milk exposure is reassuring, but is not a guarantee of zero risk.

Why a leaflet may give different advice

Some diclofenac suppository product labels advise against breastfeeding use, whereas specialist breastfeeding guidance considers clinically appropriate use acceptable. This reflects different information and approaches to risk assessment; neither a generic online statement nor a different brand’s leaflet decides your treatment. Ask the prescriber or pharmacist to reconcile the exact product’s label with your circumstances and local guidance.

Do not stop breastfeeding, discard milk, change the dose or switch medicines solely because you read conflicting advice. Agree a plan. Watch for a baby feeding less well than usual, vomiting or diarrhoea and seek advice promptly; a baby who is unusually difficult to wake or having breathing trouble needs immediate emergency assessment.

Conditions that can make diclofenac unsuitable

Do not use diclofenac if you are allergic to it or an ingredient, or if aspirin or another NSAID has triggered asthma, swelling or hives. Tell the prescriber about all drug allergies; an unrelated allergy does not automatically prohibit diclofenac. This suppository is contraindicated with active or recurrent gastrointestinal ulcer or bleeding, previous NSAID-related gastrointestinal bleeding or perforation, severe kidney or liver failure, or proctitis (inflammation of the rectum). Rectal bleeding needs assessment before further use.

Systemic diclofenac is contraindicated in established ischaemic heart disease, peripheral arterial disease, cerebrovascular disease and certain heart failure categories under UK safety advice. High blood pressure, smoking, diabetes or other cardiovascular risks need assessment. Also discuss asthma, Crohn’s disease or ulcerative colitis, clotting or bleeding disorders, a clot history and dehydration. Pregnancy is a separate issue from breastfeeding: do not self-start if pregnant or possibly pregnant; it is usually avoided in pregnancy and is contraindicated in the last trimester under this product label.

Other medicines: bleeding, blood pressure and kidneys

Give the clinician or pharmacist a complete list of prescription, non-prescription and topical medicines, vitamins, herbs and supplements. Do not add another NSAID such as ibuprofen, naproxen, ketorolac, celecoxib, indomethacin or meloxicam, or pain-relief aspirin, unless specifically advised. Check cold and pain remedies for hidden ingredients. Do not independently stop prescribed low-dose aspirin or an anticoagulant.

Anticoagulants such as warfarin, heparin or enoxaparin, antiplatelet drugs, SSRI antidepressants and corticosteroids such as prednisolone or dexamethasone can increase bleeding concerns. ACE inhibitors such as captopril/enalapril, ARBs such as losartan and diuretics such as furosemide can interact with NSAIDs, affecting blood pressure, fluid balance or kidneys, particularly during dehydration.

Other interactions and supplements

Diclofenac can affect the handling or risks of lithium, digoxin, methotrexate and phenytoin. Ciclosporin and tacrolimus require particular kidney-risk review; other potentially kidney-affecting treatments, including tenofovir, vancomycin or aminoglycoside antibiotics, also need checking in context. Vancomycin is not an aminoglycoside. Quinolone antibiotics such as ciprofloxacin can increase seizure concerns when combined with NSAIDs.

Also mention bisphosphonates such as alendronate, salicylate-containing products, glucosamine, omega-3 supplements and vitamin E. Risks and evidence differ between products and doses: this is a medication-review list, not a claim that every combination is forbidden. Other medicines may need monitoring, dose changes or an alternative; do not make those changes yourself.

Using a prescribed rectal suppository

Follow the instructions for your exact strength and prescription. If needed, use the toilet first; wash your hands, gently clean and dry the area and unwrap the suppository. Insert it gently into the rectum, pointed end first, as the leaflet directs; do not force it. It must not be swallowed or inserted into the vagina. Wash your hands afterwards.

NHS instructions advise sitting or lying still for about 15 minutes. If a dose comes out, absorption is uncertain: do not automatically insert another, even if it happened within 30 minutes. Ask a pharmacist or prescriber what to do. Never double a missed dose; if the next is nearly due, follow advice to skip the missed one. Taking or using more than prescribed needs urgent medical or poison-service advice, even if you feel well.

Side effects that need discussion

Possible effects include nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, indigestion, gas or belching, constipation, appetite change, headache, dizziness, sleepiness, rash or rectal irritation. Not everyone develops them, and not every symptom is caused by diclofenac. Discuss persistent or troublesome symptoms; do not drive or operate machinery if dizzy, sleepy or your vision is affected. For a new rash, stop diclofenac and seek prompt clinical advice before any further dose. Blistering or peeling skin, sores in the mouth or eyes, or breathing difficulty or face/throat swelling need immediate emergency care.

New hearing changes or ringing in the ears, sleep or mood changes, unexplained weight loss, unusual weakness or pallor also need review. Seek urgent medical advice for markedly reduced urine, new swelling or rapid weight gain, jaundice, unusual bruising or bleeding, hives or worsening abdominal symptoms. Cloudy urine alone is not a diagnosis, but urine changes with illness or reduced output should not be ignored.

Serious symptoms need urgent or emergency care

Black tarry stools, rectal bleeding or severe persistent indigestion or abdominal pain need urgent assessment now; do not take another dose until a clinician advises. Vomiting blood or material like coffee grounds, fainting or loss of consciousness, or severe abdominal pain with faintness needs immediate emergency care. These are not ordinary side effects to watch at home.

Chest pain, sudden shortness of breath, stroke symptoms such as one-sided weakness or difficulty speaking, or a severe allergic reaction with face/tongue/throat swelling or breathing difficulty needs immediate emergency care. Do not drive yourself. Severe illness, swelling with breathlessness or sudden major vision changes also warrants immediate assessment. After childbirth, serious symptoms may have causes other than the medicine: do not assume they are harmless drug effects.

Agreeing a practical treatment plan

Ask why this medicine and route were chosen, the exact strength and timing, how long to use it, whether other pain relief is appropriate and when pain should be reassessed. A persistent or worsening headache, wound pain, fever or other postnatal symptom may need examination rather than more pain medicine.

Keep the medicine away from children, follow the leaflet’s storage instructions and keep an updated medicine list. Breastfeeding compatibility does not remove the need to check contraindications and interactions. A pharmacist, prescriber and, when needed, a specialist breastfeeding-medicines service can help balance effective pain relief with the parent’s and baby’s safety.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

NHS/SPS guidance supports clinically appropriate diclofenac use during breastfeeding, mainly for healthy term infants; limited evidence and special infant circumstances require individual assessment.

LactMed’s 15 July 2026 review describes low milk exposure and notes that better-studied alternatives may be preferred for newborn or premature infants.

The September 2025 UK product information advises against breastfeeding use. Discuss this difference with the prescriber rather than changing treatment or feeding on your own.

NHS dosing and side-effect advice and MHRA systemic-diclofenac restrictions support careful use, interaction review and clear urgent-care advice.

How BeMama can help

Use BeMama to keep a medicine list, dose times, pain symptoms and questions about breastfeeding or the baby’s feeding. A record cannot determine whether a medicine or dose is safe for your family, or replace urgent care.

When to seek help

Do not combine NSAIDs, repeat an expelled dose, double a missed dose or change prescribed blood thinners yourself. Suspected gastrointestinal bleeding needs urgent assessment and no further diclofenac until clinical advice. Vomiting blood, fainting or loss of consciousness, chest pain, sudden breathing difficulty, stroke symptoms or severe allergy needs immediate emergency care. A baby who is difficult to wake or struggling to breathe needs immediate emergency assessment.

Evidence notes updated: October 11, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Diclofenac can be appropriate during breastfeeding; it is not universally a last-resort medicine.
  • Premature, unwell or very young babies and multiple medicines need individual assessment.
  • Rectal diclofenac acts throughout the body and retains stomach, kidney, bleeding and heart risks.
  • Check all medicines and supplements; do not automatically repeat an expelled suppository or double a missed dose.
  • Bleeding, chest or breathing symptoms, fainting or loss of consciousness or a serious allergic reaction require prompt urgent or emergency care.

Frequently asked questions

What is a diclofenac suppository?

It is a rectal form of an NSAID that reduces pain and inflammation. It enters the bloodstream and is not interchangeable with tablets, injections or skin products without checking the prescription.

Can it be used while breastfeeding?

Often yes, when clinically appropriate. NHS/SPS guidance is reassuring for a healthy term infant, but evidence is limited and some labels advise against use. Confirm the exact product and personal plan with a prescriber or pharmacist.

What if my baby is premature or unwell?

Get individual advice before treatment. LactMed notes that an alternative with more evidence may be preferable for a newborn or premature baby. Several medicines or an unwell baby also warrant specialist assessment.

Which conditions or medicines need checking?

Important issues include NSAID allergy, ulcers or bleeding, heart/vascular disease, kidney/liver disease, rectal inflammation, asthma, inflammatory bowel disease and possible pregnancy. Other NSAIDs, blood thinners, steroids, antidepressants, blood-pressure medicines and many other treatments need review.

Should I repeat a dose that comes out?

Do not automatically repeat it: some medicine may already have been absorbed. Ask a pharmacist or prescriber for advice based on the product and timing. Never double a missed dose or exceed the prescribed total.

Can I stop breastfeeding to avoid any exposure?

Do not stop or discard milk solely because of a general online warning. Ask for an individual plan that considers treatment needs, the exact product and the benefits of breastfeeding.

What should I watch for in my baby?

Contact a clinician if feeding worsens, or vomiting or diarrhoea occurs. Breathing difficulty or unusual difficulty waking needs immediate emergency assessment, whatever the suspected cause.

Which symptoms in the parent are an emergency?

Vomiting blood, fainting or loss of consciousness, chest pain, sudden breathlessness, stroke symptoms or face/throat swelling with breathing trouble need immediate emergency care. Black tarry stools, rectal bleeding or severe persistent abdominal symptoms need urgent assessment now. Do not take another dose while waiting for clinical advice about suspected bleeding.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
